title: Tazria: wait seven days (Leviticus 13:4–6)
hookLine: when unsure, the priest waits a week and looks again

lines: WHAT TO DO WITH NOT KNOWING.
cards: An email sent at eleven at night can read very differently at nine the next morning. So can a verdict on someone made on their worst day, before their next week has a chance to prove it wrong.
Speed feels like decisiveness; sometimes it's just impatience wearing a suit. The priest in Leviticus thirteen has looked carefully, in good light, and sometimes he still can't tell.
The spot is white, but not deeper than the skin, and the hair hasn't turned. It could go either way. The Torah tells him exactly what to do with not knowing.

teach.b: When the signs are unclear, the priest shuts the person away for seven days. The Hebrew verb is hisgir, to shut in or close up. He doesn't declare them unclean, and he doesn't declare them clean.
On the seventh day the priest looks again. If the spot has spread, now he knows. If it hasn't, he waits another seven days and looks a third time.
Only then, if it has faded and stayed put, is the person declared clean, washes their clothes, and goes home. Two weeks, at most, in this passage. The waiting protects two things.
A hasty verdict of unclean would send someone outside the camp for nothing; a hasty clean would miss something real.

teach.h: A KINDNESS TO PERSON AND TRUTH.
teach.b: The week is a kindness to both the person and the truth. The Torah builds in time because first looks can be wrong, even an expert's.
Pirkei Avot, the sayings of the sages, opens with the chain of tradition from Sinai, and the first advice in it is for judges: be deliberate in judgment. Slow down.
The priest with his calendar is a picture of that advice: not stuck forever in maybe, and not rushing to certainty either.
A set time, and then a fresh look. A week is long enough for a lot of things to show what they really are.

how: Pirkei Avot is traditionally studied on Shabbat afternoons in the summer, and its first advice is to be deliberate in judgment, and Jewish courts traditionally avoid rushing a verdict.

games.why: the Torah's answer to uncertainty is a set time and a second look, not a guess.

practice: Bring to mind something you've been about to decide quickly: a reply, a purchase, a judgment about someone, a plan to quit something. Ask whether it's clear, or whether you're unsure and pretending not to be.
If you're unsure, picture giving it a set time, a week or even one night, and looking again then with fresh eyes.
